title: Introduce headroom surge allocator and utilization decomposition exporter
author: Avery Chen
release_notes: Added a new headroom-based surge allocator and a utilization decomposition exporter. No customer-facing API changes. Improves tail latency stability under short spikes and provides richer telemetry for per-tenant utilization analysis.
description:
Context and motivation: customers using Dedicated fleets reported intermittent P95 regressions during microbursts. Existing warm-pool and proportional allocators reduce long-term oversubscription but react too slowly to short surge windows. This PR introduces a headroom surge allocator: a short-lived, lease-based headroom slab that can be granted to tenants for fast, low-latency bursts without disrupting long-term capacity guarantees.

Goals: 1) Provide transient capacity that keeps P95 stable during sub-minute spikes. 2) Maintain fairness and overall throughput guarantees by ensuring surge slabs are ephemeral and reconciled with long-term reservations. 3) Surface decomposition telemetry so SRE/product can attribute utilization changes to sustained vs. transient activity.

What changed (high-level): - New controller redwood/fleet/surge_allocator that manages ephemeral "headroom slabs". Slabs are issued as short leases (default 45s) and tracked separately from reservations. - Lease smoothing: allocator applies an exponentially-weighted smoothing window and a reservoir cap to avoid oscillation when spikes are frequent. - Signal fusion: autoscaler now consumes a fused signal combining request rate, observed KV-cache-hit-adjusted token-rate, and sequence-length-weighted concurrency (seqlen-weighted RPS). This reduces false positives from large batch requests. - Fallbacks: when headroom exhausted allocator emits a soft-fail marker causing graceful degrade routes to opt for lower-cost model variants. - Telemetry: introduced exporter redwood.telemetry.util_decomp which reports per-tenant breakdown: sustained_alloc, transient_surge_alloc, cache_credits_used, and effective_concurrency. Also added histogram metrics for transient_alloc_duration and per-tenant surge_success_rate.

Design notes: - Lease semantics: slab leases are time-bound and replenished after a cooldown period. We avoid hard preemption; instead we prefer proportional dampening (reduce new lease grant rate) when global utilization > threshold. - Fairness: an allocation window enforces per-tenant caps that are a function of committed reservation * and a small transient multiplier (configurable via feature flag). - Safety: a global reservoir prevents uncontrolled total transient capacity; reservoir filling is controlled by long-term idle capacity and expected decommit timings.

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for allocator logic, lease expiry, and reservoir accounting. - Integration harness (perf-canary job) simulated microbursts across 500 tenants: observed P95 token latency reduction from baseline 372ms to 341ms (≈8.3%) while overall throughput unchanged. Transient capacity usage averaged 12% of cluster for 10s windows and returned to baseline within configured cooldown. - Load tests included failure scenarios (controller restart, partial partition) to validate idempotency and lease reconciliation.

Migration and rollout: - Feature flag: "surge_allocator_v1" off by default. Gradual rollout recommended: enable on 5% of fleets, monitor redwood.telemetry.util_decomp.surge_success_rate and p95 latency. - No client-facing API changes. Console: new per-tenant "transient utilization" chart added under Dedicated -> Pools (opt-in metric).

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Perf canary run - [x] Telemetry dashboards updated - [x] Docs entry (internal runbook)

Related work: ties into ENG-6421 (protect P95 during microbursts) and ENG-6498 (telemetry for tenant utilization).
